This substantial size is likely linked to the challenging foraging environment of the tropical Atlantic, where efficient long-range flight and the ability to store energy are critical for survival. The contrast between the initial hatchling mass and the fledging mass underscores the staggering nutritional demands placed upon the provisioning adults.

Longevity and the timing of maturation are critical elements of the species' slow life-history strategy. The maximum lifespan of the Ascension frigatebird is estimated at approximately 27.6 years [am = approximately 27.6 years] when considered at an active body temperature of 40.6 °C [T = 40.6 °C], a value consistent with the extended longevity reported for the related Fregata minor. This exceptional longevity, among the highest for any seabird relative to body size, allows for repeated breeding attempts over a long lifetime. However, a price is paid in delayed maturation. Puberty, defined by the onset of gonadal maturation, is estimated to occur at 462 days after birth [tp = 462 days after birth] under the same warm thermal conditions. This extended juvenile period is typical of birds that invest heavily in a few, high-quality offspring and navigate a risky foraging landscape. The physiological mechanisms that underpin this slow development likely involve a reduced metabolic rate relative to other birds of similar mass.

The reproductive timeline of the Ascension frigatebird is marked by extreme delays. Observational data, again anchored by studies of the congeneric Fregata minor, indicate that the first successful breeding event typically occurs at 1,826 days after birth (1826 days after birth) [tR = 1826 days after birth] under the species' characteristic active thermal regime. This means that a bird hatched today will not raise its own chick for nearly five years, a staggeringly long pre-reproductive period that necessitates exceptional survival rates during the juvenile and subadult phases. The time spent as an immature individual, ranging from a recently fledged chick to a sexually mature adult, is therefore the longest demographic stage. This inherent biological constraint means that the maximum reproductive rate is extremely low, as females can only invest in a single egg every other year after reaching maturity, a strategy that buffers the population against short-term environmental fluctuations but makes it highly vulnerable to prolonged perturbations that increase adult mortality.

The foraging ecology of the Ascension frigatebird is intrinsically linked to its slow life history and the thermal environment of its tropical habitat. The high ambient temperatures, consistently around 40.6 °C [T = 40.6 °C] during activity, impose significant thermal challenges on a bird that cannot land on water. To shed heat, individuals employ gular fluttering and resort to kleptoparasitism, stealing fish from boobies and terns, a behavior that requires considerable agility. Fully-grown females of this species reach a peak body mass of 1.25 kilograms [Wwi = 1.25 kilograms], a value that underscores the demanding energy budget required to support such a large-bodied seabird in a resource-poor tropical ocean. The species' strategy of producing exactly one offspring per nesting attempt [N_R_i = one offspring per nesting attempt] represents an extreme of iteroparous life-history investment. These reproductive events are spaced at intervals of approximately twenty-four months [F_R_i = intervals of approximately twenty-four months], a remarkably slow tempo even among long-lived procellariiform and pelecaniform seabirds.
